title: Hello, what's your name?
title_target: Xin chào! Anh tên là gì?
goal: Greet people with the right pronoun, say your name and where you're from, and see for yourself that Vietnamese chooses pronouns by age — not by level of politeness.
bekal: greet with *chào* + a pronoun, and know why Vietnamese people rarely use plain *xin chào*
state your name, nationality and job with *là*
choose *anh*, *chị*, *em*, *cô*, *chú* correctly when you meet someone for the first time

dialogs.intro: A café on the shore of Hồ Tây (West Lake), Hà Nội. Budi, an Indonesian student who has lived there for just two months, is sitting alone. A woman about his age greets him from the next table.

notes: **Xin chào is a textbook greeting, not a people greeting.** It is correct and polite, but native speakers almost always use *chào* + **the pronoun**: *chào anh*, *chào chị*, *chào em*. Keep *xin chào* for groups or for when you're not yet sure what to call someone — on your first day you'll use it a lot.

**Chào is used for arriving and for leaving**, like Italian *ciao*. Even better: in everyday use there are **no time-of-day greetings**. No "good morning" or "good evening" to choose between as in English or German. Just *chào*, from dawn to midnight.

**Pronouns are chosen by age, and you can't leave them out.** There is no neutral word like English "you": you **have to** decide whether the other person is older (*anh/chị*), younger (*em*), or your parents' age (*chú/cô*). Skipping it isn't just less polite — the sentence is incomplete.
**Tôi tên là Budi is literally "I name be Budi".** *Tôi* stands as the owner, *tên* as the thing, with no "my" or "of" — like saying "me, name: Budi". A very common short form: *Tôi tên Budi*.

**Vâng, dạ and ừ are three levels of "yes".** *Vâng* is polite and standard (northern); *dạ* is even more respectful (typically southern, understood everywhere) — use it with people much older than you; *ừ* is casual and **only downward**. Saying *ừ* to an older person sounds rude.

**Quá and lắm stand AFTER the adjective**, while their cousin *rất* stands **before**: *giỏi quá* = *giỏi lắm* = *rất giỏi* = "very good". The feel differs: *rất* describes, *quá* and *lắm* come from the heart — which is why compliments almost always use *quá* or *lắm*.

grammars.title: Personal pronouns — choose by age
body: This is the one part of Vietnamese that really is more complicated than English — but the idea isn't foreign. You already adjust how you address people: "sir", "ma'am", "auntie", "Grandpa", a first name. Vietnamese does the same, only **with no neutral way out** — the choice *is* the word for "you".

after: ⚠️ **The same word is used for "I" and for "you".** If the other person is older, you call him *anh* and call yourself *em*; he calls himself *anh* and calls you *em*. It looks confusing on the page; in conversation it feels clear, because each person has only one option.

**When in doubt: *tôi* for yourself, *anh/chị* for the other person.** Treating someone as slightly older is almost always taken as respect; the reverse is what hurts. **A first name can also replace the pronoun** — *Linh đi đâu?* for "where are you going?", said to Linh herself, the way a parent might ask a child "Is Linh hungry?".

grammars.title: Là — links two nouns, and that's all
body: *Là* means "to be", and its job is very narrow: it links **a noun to a noun**. Before an adjective it is **not used** — and that is exactly where beginners trip most often.
after: ⚠️ **Negating *là* takes three words: *không phải là*** — literally "not right be". Not *không là*. It is the only Vietnamese negation where *không* alone isn't enough, and the whole form has to be memorized as a unit.

So Vietnamese has two kinds of "not": *không phải là* before a noun ("I'm **not** a student") and plain *không* before an adjective or verb ("the house is**n't** nice"). Ask yourself: is there a noun after "be"? Then it's *không phải là*.

blocks.text: ⚠️ *Chúc ngủ ngon* literally means "wish sleep tasty" and is only used when the person is actually going to bed — not as "good evening" when meeting. To greet someone in the evening, it's still *chào*.

blocks.title: One Vietnamese habit to know in advance
items: Questions about age, marital status and job come **much earlier** than in English-speaking countries — often within the first five minutes. That's not nosiness; it's a grammatical need. The other person is working out whether to call you *anh*, *chú* or *em*, and can't build a sentence until they know.
So it's best to answer "how old are you?" plainly. Dodging it only leaves the other person stuck.

sections.title: Nationality, country, language — one pattern for all three

blocks.text: ⚠️ Notice that *Anh* means "England" **and** "older brother". Two completely different words with exactly the same spelling and tone; only their place in the sentence tells them apart. Vietnamese is full of pairs like this — the price of a language where almost every word is one syllable.

*Xin* in front of a verb means "I beg" and turns a command into a polite request: *nói lại* = "say again", *xin nói lại* = "please say that again". It works like English "please", except it always goes first.
